newsitem.title: USA: Environment may decide many U.S. elections - survey.
newsitem.headline: Environment may decide many U.S. elections - survey.

text.p: A clean air group, backed by a poll showing that the environment can be a deciding factor for voters, said Tuesday that candidates' environmental records may decide a number of elections across the country.

Thirty-three percent of voters surveyed in the poll released by the Clean Air Trust said the environment was a primary factor in deciding how to vote. Another 52 percent said it was one of several issues they would consider.

"The public debate has focused more on issues like Medicare, the balanced budget, welfare and minimum wage, yet this survey of the national electorate and five pivotal states shows that the perception of an anti-environmental record can be the deciding factor in races across the country," said the report by Democratic pollster Greenberg Research Inc.

Candidates' environmental records could decide Senate races in Oregon, Arkansas and New Hampshire, it said, with Democrats Dick Swett in New Hampshire, Tom Bruggere in Oregon and Winston Bryant in Arkansas gaining leads when voters heard comments on their opponents' environmental records.
In the other sample states, incumbent Democratic Sens. Tom Harkin of Iowa and Max Baucus of Montana increased their leads when their opponents' environmental records were raised, the survey said.

In a briefing, pollster Stanley Greenberg said the survey also showed 57 percent of voters favoured tougher air standards to protect children with asthma. Support for stiffer standards held even when people were reminded of possible results in higher costs for gasoline and auto emissions inspections and constraints on job growth, Greenberg said.

Women were far more concerned about air pollution, the survey showed, with 64 percent supporting tougher air quality standards compared with 50 percent of men. The strongest worries on air pollution were found among women without college degrees, which Greenberg said should dispel ideas the environment is largely an upscale, suburban issue.
The national survey of 751 people conducted Sept. 9-12 had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent, meaning results could vary either way by four percentage points.
